title: The shield and the judge
hook: a well-known report: Ali loses a case against a Christian over a shield, because he has no witness, and the man becomes Muslim

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Kharijites, who went out and declared other Muslims unbelievers. Your line was not our place to declare.

A stall in the market of Kufa, and on it, for sale, a piece of battle gear. A man walking past stops. He knows it. It's his. It went missing, and here it is, in the hands of a Christian trader. The man walking past is Ali, commander of the faithful, ruler of the Muslims. He could have it taken with a word. Instead, the story goes, he says: let's go to the judge. This well-known report is more about the judge than the shield.
screen: `A STALL IN KUFA.` → `THAT'S MINE.` → `LET'S GO TO THE JUDGE.`

segments.voice: The judge is Shurayh, appointed by the caliphs. The caliph walks in as an ordinary party to a case, and in some tellings he gently objects when Shurayh shows him more respect than the other man. Ali says: it's mine. The trader says: it's mine, and it's in my hand. Shurayh asks Ali for witnesses. Ali brings his son Hasan, and in some tellings his servant Qanbar too. The judge says he will not accept a son's testimony for his father. Ali has no further proof, so Shurayh rules for the trader. The caliph lost the case, before his own judge, in his own city. The trader walks out with the gear, then turns back. The ruler of the Muslims, he says, brought me before his own judge, and the judge ruled against him. He says the gear really is Ali's, that it fell from his camel on the road, and he declares himself a Muslim. In the story, Ali gives it to him as a gift. Now the careful part. The report is found in later collections, such as al-Bayhaqi's, and hadith scholars have questioned the strength of its chain. Some tellings make the trader a Jewish man rather than a Christian, and the gear is often a coat of mail rather than a shield. So it's best heard as a report the tradition loves, not a sealed record. What it keeps alive is a command the Qur'an gives: when you judge between people, judge with justice. Shurayh did, even with the caliph standing before him.
screen: `THE CALIPH AS AN ORDINARY PARTY.` · `NO SON'S TESTIMONY FOR HIS FATHER.` · `THE TRADER TURNS BACK.` · `A LOVED REPORT, A QUESTIONED CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE CALIPH LOST THE CASE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent decision that went against you through a fair process: a referee's call, a review at work, a family vote, a friend who said honestly that you were wrong. Notice whether part of you is still arguing the case, and let the ruling stand; you can be sure you were right and still honor a fair process. If you pray, you can ask for a just heart.
Qadi, a judge: Shurayh, before whom Ali, as caliph, lost a case for lack of a witness, and the other man, moved by the fairness, became Muslim. Today's word.
Your line: the caliph lost the case. Power stood before the judge like anyone else. Case closed for today.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the report of Ali and the judge Shurayh when teaching that rulers stand equal before the law, while noting that hadith scholars have questioned its chain.

chat.says: Why do people still tell the story of Ali and the shield?
options: Because a caliph went to court as an ordinary party, and lost fairly.
Because it proves the shield belonged to the trader all along.
Because Ali punished the judge who ruled against him.
chat.meaning: Shurayh would not accept a son's testimony for his father and ruled for the trader. The report's chain is questioned, but it keeps alive judging with justice.

Kufa.meaning: the city in Iraq where Ali ruled

al-Bayhaqi.meaning: a later hadith scholar whose collection keeps the report

notes: Audit: 'Ali has no other proof' contradicted the tellings in which Qanbar also testifies; the teach now mentions Qanbar in some tellings and says Ali had no further proof (one witness short).
The report's chain is weak by many hadith scholars' assessment; the script says so and calls it 'a report the tradition loves'. Confirm phrasing and the source references (al-Bayhaqi, Abu Nu'aym).

Variants: the trader is Christian in some tellings and Jewish in others; the item is usually dir' (coat of mail). The index says 'shield' and 'Christian'; the script follows the index and notes the variants. Consider renaming the index word to 'the armor and the judge'.
Some versions name Qanbar as a second witness whom Shurayh accepts, leaving Ali one witness short; the script simplifies to Hasan only. Confirm.
The conversion is told without framing it against Christianity; confirm the tone is welcoming to Christian listeners.
The hook calls it 'a well-known report', following the index.
